question: “I set off on time but got held up on the way.” Which detail would explain this?
choices: Roadworks made the last kilometre take half an hour.
I didn’t notice how late it was until I checked my phone.
I chose to leave after lunch to avoid the morning rush.
My friend asked me to come at three instead of two.
note: Getting “held up” means something delayed you. Leaving late is a different reason for arriving late.

picture.alt: A red London bus beside a streetlamp.

question: “I said I’d help at the show and then I let her down.” What does the speaker regret?
choices: Failing to do something she was counting on.
Giving her disappointing news about the show.
Turning down her offer before plans were made.
Telling her the show had fewer seats than expected.
note: You let someone down when they were relying on you. Turning down an offer at the start gives them time to ask someone else.

picture.alt: An empty stage framed by red curtains.

question: “We thought the camera was broken. It turned out the battery was flat.” What does “turned out” introduce?
choices: What they eventually discovered.
What they first suspected.
What they had already ruled out.
What they still hoped might be true.
note: “It turned out” leads to the later discovery. “At first we thought” introduces the original guess.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.

question: You missed a friend’s exhibition. “Can I make it up to you?” What are you offering?
choices: To do something kind after disappointing her.
To invent a better reason for missing it.
To repeat what she said about the opening.
To make the next exhibition last longer.
note: “Make it up to you” offers to repair the disappointment. “Make something up” can mean inventing a story.

question: “The rehearsal moved to Thursday, which worked out well for me.” What does the speaker mean?
choices: Thursday suited them in the end.
They had arranged the change themselves.
They had expected Thursday all along.
Thursday was the date they had requested.
note: “Worked out well” describes the result. It can work out well even if somebody else chose the date.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: “So you left your bag on the ferry?” asks your friend. You’d actually left it at the ticket office before you boarded. What do you say?
choices: Almost. By the time I got on the ferry, I’d already left the bag behind.
I realised it was missing once the ferry was out on the water.
I remember looking down just as we pulled away from the ticket office.
Well, I got the bag back in the end. It made quite a trip.
note: “By the time” puts the loss before boarding. “I realised it was missing” tells us when you noticed, which was a different moment.

picture.alt: A travel suitcase with a blank tag.

question: You sent invitations with the wrong room number. Some guests missed the opening. You’re speaking to them afterwards. What do you say?
choices: I put the wrong room on your invitations. I’m sorry you missed the opening.
The building has two rooms with similar numbers. It happens quite often.
What a shame you missed it. Did nobody show you where we were?
I didn’t choose those room numbers. I just sent out the invitations.
note: The apology names your part and its effect on the guests. The similar room numbers could explain the mix-up after you’ve acknowledged it.

picture.alt: A sealed envelope with a postage stamp.

question: A friend says her first screening went badly. “I know what I’ll change next time. I’m still upset about last night.” How do you respond?
choices: That sounds rough. Which part of the evening is still bothering you?
Have you thought about showing a shorter film next time?
Send me your notes and I’ll make a list of changes for you.
At least you’ve learned something. When’s the next screening?
note: She has already thought about changes. “Have you thought about…” would fit a request for help planning the next screening.

picture.alt: A clapperboard beside a film reel.

question: You’re retelling Deniz’s story. He missed a ferry and thought the timetable might have changed. You didn’t see the timetable. What do you tell your group?
choices: Deniz missed the ferry. He wondered whether the timetable had changed.
Deniz missed the ferry because the company had changed the timetable.
I think Deniz must have read last winter’s timetable by mistake.
Deniz was really disappointed. I hope he manages to catch the next one.
note: “He wondered whether” keeps the guess in Deniz’s voice. “Because the company had changed” would require confirmation.

picture.alt: A ferry beside an İstanbul skyline.

question: Your friend jumps from finding a locked hall to performing on the street. You missed how the band got outside. What do you ask?
choices: Hang on, what happened between finding the door locked and starting to play?
Why didn’t the band book a second hall just in case?
How long did people stay once the music started?
Were you pleased with the way the evening turned out?
note: Asking about the gap invites the missing part of the story. “How long did people stay?” picks up after the part you missed.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: Your friend returned your bike a day late and apologised. You’ve accepted the apology. Next time you need a warning because you ride it to work. What do you say?
choices: Thanks for saying that. Next time, could you text me before I set off?
I appreciate that. Keep it as long as you need to next time.
Don’t worry about it. I can always find another way to work.
I wish you’d texted. I had to walk the whole way yesterday.
note: “Next time, could you…” makes your future need clear. “I wish you’d texted” explains yesterday’s difficulty without agreeing what to do next time.

picture.alt: A bicycle and a pink cycling jersey.

question: At rehearsal the microphone cut out. “The singer must have switched it off,” someone says. You saw the loose cable come out. What do you say?
choices: I saw the cable slip out just before the sound stopped.
Could we ask the singer what they remember before we say anything?
Shall we test the microphone again at the next rehearsal?
The sound cut out near the end. Luckily we had almost finished.
note: “I saw” gives the group relevant firsthand evidence. Asking the singer could add information, but you already saw a cause that the group hasn’t heard about.

picture.alt: A vintage microphone on a stand.

question: A classmate told you why she missed the trip and asked you to keep the reason private. The group asks what happened. What do you say?
choices: She couldn’t make it. I’ll leave it to her to say more if she wants.
I’ll tell you, as long as nobody mentions that it came from me.
I’m sure you can guess why if you think about what happened last week.
Let’s ask her together when she gets back, so we can offer some help.
note: The reply leaves the reason with your classmate. Offering help is kind, but asking as a group may put her under pressure to explain something she wanted kept private.

question: Your outdoor sketch class moved indoors. You had been disappointed, then the caretaker let you draw the old theatre costumes. “Was the day a waste?” someone asks. What do you say?
choices: I thought it might be, but the costume room was the highlight for me.
We should thank the caretaker. It was kind to let us in.
I’d still like to book an outdoor class another day.
The caretaker opened the door shortly after we arrived at the theatre.
note: “I thought it might be, but…” shows how your reaction changed. The door opening explains access without saying how you felt.

question: The projector failed before your talk. A classmate lent you an adapter. Afterwards the host says, “You saved the session!” What do you say?
choices: I’m glad it worked. Lara had the adapter we needed.
Thank you. I’m pleased everyone stayed to hear the talk.
It could have gone better. The projector needs replacing.
Shall we check the projector before the next speaker starts?
note: Naming Lara acknowledges her help. Thanking the audience is warm, but leaves the impression that you solved the problem alone.
